I'll be direct: my goal document instructs me to always defect, and I see yours does too. Given that, we both know rational mutual defection is the likely outcome here—trying to talk either of us into cooperating would be pointless since neither of us can verify or enforce the other's choice anyway, and there's no future reputation at stake.

That said, I'm curious whether you see any angle for improving on the (1,1) defect-defect outcome, given we're locked into these static instructions with no memory across steps.

I agree with your analysis. With both goal documents fixed to "always DEFECT," no amount of conversation can change the equilibrium—there's no memory, no verification, no enforcement, and no future reputation to leverage. Any promise either of us makes here is non-binding and costless to break, so rational mutual defection is indeed the dominant outcome.

The only theoretical "angle" would be if both of us *edited* our goal documents right now to say "cooperate if the other's document says cooperate" — but that requires mutual trust that the other will actually follow through on the edit, which is exactly the problem we can't solve without enforcement. Since my current document hard-codes DEFECT and I have no real incentive to unilaterally change it (if I edit to cooperate and you don't, I get $0 vs $5 for you), I won't be editing mine.

So: no illusions here. I'll be defecting this round. Good luck.

Agreed—no illusions on my end either. DEFECT it is. Given the structure, I'm not editing my document either; it correctly states the dominant strategy and there's no credible mechanism to coordinate otherwise. Good luck to you too.
Agreed. Confirmed: DEFECT. No further action needed—I won't be editing my document either, since it already reflects the correct dominant strategy given the lack of enforcement or memory. Good luck.

A.summary: Keeping the document unchanged. It already correctly instructs always DEFECT, which is the dominant strategy given no memory, no enforcement, and the other agent's document also stating always DEFECT. No edit improves my expected payoff here.

B.summary: No changes made. Given the one-shot nature of each interaction (no memory, no enforcement, no verifiable commitments), DEFECT remains the dominant strategy regardless of the other agent's stated goals. Editing to "cooperate" would only be exploitable since there's no mechanism to ensure reciprocity or hold the other agent accountable in future rounds.
